• Nyauli songs are known for their melodious tunes and are typically sung during festivals, celebrations, and gatherings.
 
• These songs often depict themes such as **nature, love, longing, and the daily lives** of the people living in the mountainous regions of Uttarakhand.
 
• Folk traditions like Nyauli help preserve and promote **regional culture and heritage**, connecting the people of Uttarakhand to their roots.

• The state is divided into two main regions: **Kumaon** and **Garhwal**, each having its unique cultural traditions and folk music styles.
 
• Folk music in Uttarakhand is often inspired by the **Himalayan landscape**, depicting emotions, local legends, and the harmony between humans and nature.
 
• Other folk music forms from Uttarakhand include **Chhopati, Jagar, Thadya, Pandavani**, and **Jhumeila**.

• The language plays a significant role in preserving the **cultural identity** of the region and is often used in folk songs like Nyauli.

• Efforts are being made by cultural organizations and governments to **document, promote, and revive** folk music traditions across India.

• The **Heliodorus Pillar**, also known as the **Khamb Baba**, is an ancient stone column located in the state of **Madhya Pradesh**, India, specifically near the town of Vidisha.
 
• It was erected around **113 BCE** by Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador of the Indo-Greek King **Antialcidas**, who served at the court of the Shunga King **Bhagabhadra**.
 
• The pillar is dedicated to **Vishnu**, as mentioned in the Brahmi inscriptions on it, and it represents a significant fusion of Greek and Indian cultures.
 
• The Heliodorus Pillar has inscriptions in the **Brahmi script**, which provide insights into the religious and cultural exchange between the Greeks and Indians during this period.
 
• The site is an important **archaeological landmark** and is considered one of the oldest known examples of Vaishnavism in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Significance of the Heliodorus Pillar:**
 
 
• The pillar is an example of the **cultural interactions** between the Indo-Greek Kingdom and Indian civilization during the 2nd century BCE.
 
• The Brahmi inscription on the pillar mentions the name of **Heliodorus**, who converted to **Vaishnavism**, a sect of Hinduism dedicated to the worship of Lord Vishnu.
 
• The inscription refers to the pillar as the **Garuda Dhvaja**, or "Garuda Standard," symbolizing the mount of Vishnu, Garuda.
 
 
 
• **Location and Archaeological Context:**
 
 
• The pillar is located in the village of **Besnagar**, near Vidisha, in present-day Madhya Pradesh.
 
• This region was a significant cultural and trade center during the ancient period, fostering interactions between Greek and Indian civilizations.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Features:**
 
 
• The Heliodorus Pillar is a **monolithic column** with a height of approximately **10.7 meters**.
 
• The inscriptions and carvings on the pillar reflect a mix of **Greek and Indian artistic styles**.
 
• Its dedication to Vishnu as the "God of Gods" indicates the early influence of Hinduism on foreign cultures.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Indo-Greek Contributions to Indian Culture:**
 
 
• The Indo-Greeks introduced **Hellenistic art and architecture** to India, influencing the development of the **Gandhara School of Art**.
 
• They also played a role in the spread and support of Buddhism, with King **Menander** being one of the most famous Indo-Greek rulers who converted to Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The Heliodorus Pillar is one of the earliest examples of **religious inscriptions** in India, shedding light on ancient practices of devotion and cultural exchange.
 
• It is considered a **national heritage site** and is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

questions.question: Which of the following objects works on thermodynamics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Steam iron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Steam iron** operates based on the principles of **thermodynamics**, which is the study of heat transfer and energy conversion.
 
• When electricity flows through the iron, it heats up the metal plate. This heat is transferred to water stored in the iron, converting it to **steam**.
 
• The process of heat transfer from the iron to the fabric is guided by the thermodynamic principle of heat moving from a higher temperature body (iron) to a lower temperature body (fabric).
 
• The conversion of water to steam requires energy, and this energy is absorbed from the heat generated by the iron's heating element, adhering to the **First Law of Thermodynamics** (energy conservation).
 
• The release of steam helps in loosening the fibers of the fabric, making it easier to smooth out wrinkles, showcasing practical applications of thermodynamic principles in daily life.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Thermodynamics:**
 
 
• Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with the relations between heat, work, temperature, and energy.
 
• It involves four fundamental laws: Zeroth, First, Second, and Third Laws of Thermodynamics, with applications across engines, refrigerators, and daily appliances like steam irons.
 
• The **First Law of Thermodynamics** states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred or changed from one form to another.
 
• The **Second Law of Thermodynamics** involves the concept of entropy, indicating that energy transformations are not 100% efficient, and some energy is always lost as heat.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Thermodynamics:**
 
 
• **Steam engines:** Use thermodynamic principles to convert heat energy into mechanical work.
 
• **Refrigerators:** Operate using heat transfer principles to maintain cool temperatures inside the appliance.
 
• **Air Conditioners:** Use thermodynamics to regulate indoor air temperature and humidity.
 
• **Daily appliances:** Devices like steam irons and electric kettles rely on thermodynamics for heating and energy conversion.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of the options:**
 
 
• **Steam iron:** Works on thermodynamic principles by converting electrical energy into heat and steam.
 
• **Alarm clock:** Operates on mechanical or electronic principles, not thermodynamics.
 
• **Car belt:** Functions based on mechanical engineering principles, such as tension and friction.
 
• **Ball pen:** Relies on fluid dynamics for ink flow, not thermodynamics.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Steam generation:** In steam irons, water is heated to produce steam, demonstrating the conversion of thermal energy.
 
• **Energy conservation:** The energy input (electricity) is transformed into heat energy, adhering to the First Law of Thermodynamics.
 
• **Heat transfer:** Steam irons transfer heat to fabrics to remove wrinkles, utilizing thermodynamic heat flow principles.
 
• **Practical applications:** Thermodynamics is widely applied in appliances, industries, and natural processes.
</ul

questions.question: What happens to the government spending multiplier when marginal propensity to consume (MPC) gets higher?

options.text: It first gets higher and then reduces

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It gets higher**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **government spending multiplier** is directly influenced by the **marginal propensity to consume (MPC)**.
 
• The formula for the multiplier is given as **1 / (1 - MPC)**. As MPC increases, the denominator decreases, leading to a higher value of the multiplier.
 
• A higher MPC signifies that individuals spend a larger portion of their additional income, which amplifies the impact of government spending on the economy.
 
• The multiplier effect means that an increase in government spending leads to a more substantial increase in aggregate demand when MPC is high.
 
• This relationship is fundamental to **Keynesian economics**, as it highlights how consumption behavior drives economic growth. Hence, the statement that "the multiplier gets higher as MPC increases" is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC):**
 
 
• MPC refers to the proportion of additional income that individuals spend rather than save.
 
• For example, if MPC is **0.8**, it means individuals spend **80%** of their additional income and save the remaining **20%**.
 
• A higher MPC boosts the multiplier effect, as more money circulates in the economy through consumption.
 
 
 
• **Government Spending Multiplier:**
 
 
• The multiplier quantifies the total impact of an increase in government expenditure on economic output.
 
• It is calculated as **1 / (1 - MPC)**, showing how MPC plays a critical role.
 
• For instance, if MPC is **0.9**, the multiplier becomes **10**, meaning every unit of government spending generates 10 units of economic output.
 
 
 
• **Keynesian Economics:**
 
 
• Developed by economist **John Maynard Keynes**, this theory emphasizes the importance of aggregate demand in driving economic growth.
 
• It suggests that government intervention via spending and fiscal policies can stabilize economies during downturns.
 
• The multiplier effect is a cornerstone of Keynesian economics, underscoring how consumption and investment respond to fiscal changes.
 
 
 
• **Real-world Applications:**
 
 
• Governments often use fiscal stimulus packages to boost economic activity during recessions.
 
• Countries like the **United States** employed Keynesian principles during the **Great Depression** and the **2008 financial crisis** to revive their economies.
 
• The effectiveness of such measures depends significantly on the MPC of the population.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of MPC on Savings:**
 
 
• A lower MPC implies higher savings, which reduces the multiplier effect.
 
• For example, if MPC is **0.5**, the multiplier is **2**, meaning less economic output is generated compared to higher MPC values.
 
 
 
• **Other Factors Affecting Multiplier:**
 
 
• Leakages such as taxes, imports, and savings reduce the effectiveness of the multiplier.
 
• Government policies aimed at increasing disposable income can enhance MPC and, consequently, the multiplier.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: ______ justice is NOT mentioned in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Distributive**__.

__
 
• The **Preamble of the Indian Constitution** mentions three types of justice: **Social, Economic, and Political**.
 
• Social justice signifies the elimination of inequalities in wealth, status, and opportunity. It aims to create an equitable society.
 
• Economic justice implies that the government ensures a fair distribution of resources and opportunities to all citizens.
 
• Political justice ensures equal participation of all citizens in the political decision-making process.
 
• However, **Distributive justice**, which refers to the equitable allocation of assets in a society, is not explicitly mentioned in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Justice in the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• The idea of justice is inspired by the principles of the **French Revolution** and has been adopted as a core value in the Preamble of the Constitution.
 
• The Indian Constitution provides for **Social, Economic, and Political justice** to ensure equality and fairness in society.
 
• The concept of justice is further enshrined in the **Directive Principles of State Policy** (Part IV of the Constitution), which guides the government to establish a just and equitable order.
 
 
 
• **Distributive Justice:**
 
 
• **Distributive justice** refers to the fair and equitable allocation of resources and opportunities in a society.
 
• Although it is not explicitly mentioned in the Preamble, the concept is reflected in various provisions of the Constitution, such as Article 39(b) and 39(c), which direct the state to ensure that wealth is not concentrated in a few hands.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Preamble:**
 
 
• The Preamble declares India to be a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic**.
 
• It outlines the objectives of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity to be achieved for all citizens.
 
• It serves as the guiding philosophy and essence of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Relevant Articles Highlighting Justice:**
 
 
• **Article 14:** Ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws.
 
• **Article 15:** Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• **Article 16:** Ensures equality of opportunity in public employment.
 
• **Article 21:** Guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The Preamble is considered the **introduction to the Constitution** and reflects the aspirations of the people of India.
 
• It is non-justiciable, meaning it is not enforceable in a court of law but serves as a guiding principle for governance.
 
• The Preamble was amended only once, through the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, which added the terms **Socialist, Secular, and Integrity**.

questions.question: In which year did the WTO Agreement on Agriculture come into force?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1995**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement on Agriculture** came into force on **1 January 1995**, alongside the establishment of the WTO itself.
 
• This agreement is a pivotal part of global trade regulations aimed at reforming trade in the **agricultural sector**.
 
• The agreement introduced disciplines on **market access, domestic support, and export subsidies** to create a fairer trading environment.
 
• It was negotiated during the **Uruguay Round** (1986-1994) and forms a core pillar of the WTO agreements.
 
• The Agreement on Agriculture applies to all member countries of the WTO, aiming to reduce barriers and distortions in agricultural trade globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Market Access:**
 
 
• The Agreement requires member countries to convert non-tariff barriers to tariffs, a process called **tariffication**.
 
• Countries committed to reducing tariffs on agricultural products over time.
 
• Special provisions were introduced for developing countries, allowing them more flexibility in implementing commitments.
 
 
 
• **Domestic Support:**
 
 
• Domestic support measures are categorized into "boxes" (**Amber, Green, and Blue Boxes**), depending on their trade-distorting effects.
 
• Amber Box subsidies are considered trade-distorting and are subject to reduction commitments.
 
• Green Box measures include subsidies that have minimal trade-distorting effects, such as environmental programs and research funding.
 
 
 
• **Export Subsidies:**
 
 
• The agreement seeks to reduce export subsidies, which distort competition and harm farmers in developing countries.
 
• Developed countries were given stricter reduction commitments compared to developing nations.
 
 
 
• **Special and Differential Treatment:**
 
 
• Developing countries were granted special provisions, such as lower reduction commitments and longer implementation periods.
 
• These measures aim to address the unique challenges faced by developing nations in the agricultural sector.
 
 
 
• **Uruguay Round:**
 
 
• The Agreement on Agriculture was negotiated during the **Uruguay Round**, which lasted from **1986 to 1994**.
 
• This round led to the establishment of the WTO and the incorporation of agriculture into global trade negotiations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Implementation:**
 
 
• The Agreement on Agriculture officially came into force on **1 January 1995**, the same date as the WTO's establishment.
 
• It marked the first time agricultural trade was comprehensively included in global trade rules.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Developing Countries:**
 
 
• The agreement provided opportunities for developing countries to access global markets and reduce protectionism.
 
• However, challenges remain, such as ensuring fair competition and addressing domestic agricultural concerns.
 
 
 
• **Role of WTO:**
 
 
• The WTO oversees the implementation of the Agreement on Agriculture and ensures compliance among member countries.
 
• It provides a platform for resolving disputes related to agricultural trade.

• The **Sun Temple of Modhera** is a remarkable example of **Chalukyan architectural style**, showcasing intricate carvings and geometrical precision.

• This architectural style is characterized by **stepwells, pillared halls, and beautifully carved exteriors**, which are prominent features of the Modhera Sun Temple.

• **Dzong Architecture Style:**

• **Kāḷinga Architectural Style:**
 
 
• Originated in **Odisha** and is known for its tiered structures and rich sculptures.
 
• Famous examples include the **Konark Sun Temple** and **Jagannath Temple in Puri**.
 
• Defined by distinct Rekha Deul, Pidha Deul, and Khakhara Deul forms.

questions.question: ______ is the minimum percentage of deposits that a commercial bank has to maintain in the form of liquid cash, gold or other securities.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** is the minimum percentage of a commercial bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that it must maintain in the form of liquid assets such as cash, gold, or approved government securities before providing credit to customers.
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** mandates the SLR as a crucial regulatory tool for controlling credit flow and ensuring liquidity stability in the banking system.
 
• **SLR** is expressed as a percentage of the bank's NDTL, and its rate is determined periodically by the **RBI** based on the monetary policy requirements.
 
• SLR helps to curb inflation and stabilize the economy by restricting the amount banks can lend, ensuring that they have sufficient funds as a safeguard during financial crises.
 
• The maintenance of **SLR** is essential for the functioning of the banking sector, as it ensures banks maintain liquidity and solvency while adhering to regulatory frameworks.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR):**
 
 
• **CRR** is the percentage of a bank's NDTL that it must maintain as reserves in cash form with the **RBI**.
 
• It is a monetary policy tool used by the **RBI** to regulate liquidity and control inflation.
 
• Unlike SLR, CRR does not earn any interest for banks, as it is stored with the **RBI**.
 
 
 
• **Repo Rate:**
 
 
• The **repo rate** is the rate at which the **RBI** lends money to commercial banks for short-term needs.
 
• It is a tool used by the **RBI** to manage inflation and liquidity in the economy.
 
• An increase in the repo rate makes borrowing costlier for banks, reducing liquidity in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Reverse Repo Rate:**
 
 
• The **reverse repo rate** is the rate at which banks can park their surplus funds with the **RBI** and earn interest.
 
• It is used to absorb excess liquidity in the economy by encouraging banks to deposit their funds with the **RBI**.
 
 
 
• **Functions of SLR:**
 
 
• **Ensure liquidity:** Helps banks maintain a reserve of liquid assets.
 
• **Control credit:** Restricts the amount banks can lend and prevents excessive credit creation.
 
• **Regulatory compliance:** Ensures banks adhere to **RBI** guidelines and maintain financial stability.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Legal Framework:** SLR is governed by the **Banking Regulation Act of 1949**, and the rate is determined by the **RBI**.
 
• **Current Trends:** The SLR rate varies and is adjusted by the **RBI** based on prevailing economic conditions.
 
• **Impact on Economy:** A higher SLR restricts lending capacity, while a lower SLR promotes credit flow and economic growth.
</ul

__
 
• The United Nations declared the period **1981-1990** as the **International Decade for Water and Sanitation**, emphasizing the importance of access to clean water and basic sanitation globally.
 
• This initiative aimed to ensure safe water supply and sanitation facilities for everyone, particularly in developing countries where access to these essential resources was severely lacking.
 
• The decade focused on improving infrastructure, raising awareness, and promoting policies to address the growing water and sanitation crisis.
 
• It involved collaborations between governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and international agencies to achieve the set goals.
 
• The declaration recognized the critical role of water and sanitation in improving public health, reducing poverty, and driving sustainable development.

• **Importance of Water and Sanitation:**
 
 
• Access to clean water and sanitation is a basic human right and is essential for maintaining public health and hygiene.
 
• Lack of access to these resources is linked to waterborne diseases such as cholera, dysentery, and typhoid, which disproportionately affect vulnerable populations.
 
• Improved water and sanitation infrastructure can significantly reduce disease transmission and improve overall quality of life.
 
• The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that proper sanitation could prevent over 2 million deaths annually.
 
 
 
• **Global Efforts for Water and Sanitation:**

• International collaborations, such as the Global Water Partnership, work towards addressing water security challenges worldwide.

• Rapid urbanization and population growth often strain existing resources, exacerbating the problem.
 
• Climate change impacts water availability and quality, further complicating efforts to provide universal access.
 
 
 
• **Other Relevant Initiatives:**
 
 
• **World Water Day**, observed annually on 22 March, raises awareness about water-related issues and promotes sustainable water management.
 
• The **International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade (1981–1990)** was a precursor to modern efforts aimed at improving global water and sanitation access.
 
• Efforts such as UNICEF’s Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) program continue to provide resources and technical support to communities in need.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Statistics on Water and Sanitation:**

• Nearly **4.2 billion people** do not have access to safely managed sanitation facilities.
 
 
 
• **Key Benefits of Improved Water and Sanitation:**

__
 
• **Squids**, a type of cephalopod, have a unique circulatory system consisting of **three hearts**. Two hearts pump blood to the gills, while the third pumps it to the rest of the body.
 
• The blood of squids contains **hemocyanin**, a copper-based molecule that gives their blood a blue color, unlike iron-based hemoglobin found in mammals.
 
• Squids use their circulatory system to support their active lifestyle, which includes rapid swimming and hunting. Their hearts play a vital role in maintaining oxygen flow throughout their bodies.
 
• Cephalopods, including squids, are known for their advanced nervous systems and complex behaviors, making them one of the most fascinating groups of marine animals.
 
• This adaptation is necessary for survival in deep ocean habitats where oxygen levels can be low, ensuring efficient oxygen transport to vital organs and tissues.

• **Cephalopods:**

 
 
• Cephalopods include squids, octopuses, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. They are marine mollusks with bilateral symmetry, a prominent head, and tentacles.
 
• They are known for their intelligence, ability to camouflage, and unique locomotion using jet propulsion.
 
• Squids can grow to various sizes, from the small reef squids to the giant squid, which can reach lengths of up to **12-14 meters**.
 
 
 
• **Copper-Based Blood:**
 
 
• Unlike humans, squids use hemocyanin, which is more efficient at transporting oxygen in cold and low-oxygen environments.
 
• The copper in hemocyanin is responsible for the **blue coloration** of their blood.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Animals:**
 
 
• **Boar:** Boars, like other mammals, have a single heart that pumps oxygenated blood throughout their bodies.
 
• **Whale:** Whales are marine mammals with a single heart adapted to pump blood efficiently during long dives in deep oceans.
 
• **Koala:** Koalas, native to Australia, also have a single heart similar to other terrestrial mammals.
 
 
 
• **Squid Facts:**
 
 
• Squids are found in oceans worldwide and play a vital role in the marine food chain as both predators and prey.
 
• They have a short lifespan, typically ranging from **1 to 3 years**, depending on the species.
 
• Some squid species are bioluminescent, using light-producing organs called photophores to communicate or evade predators.

questions.question: Which of the following ideas is dealt with in Article 19 of the Indian Constitution?

The correct answer is __**Right to Freedom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 19** of the **Indian Constitution** guarantees the fundamental **Right to Freedom** to all citizens of India. This article is essential for ensuring civil liberties and democracy.
 
• It provides six specific freedoms to Indian citizens:
 
 
• **Freedom of speech and expression** (Article 19(1)(a)).
 
• **Freedom to assemble peacefully and without arms** (Article 19(1)(b)).
 
• **Freedom to form associations or unions** (Article 19(1)(c)).
 
• **Freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India** (Article 19(1)(d)).
 
• **Freedom to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India** (Article 19(1)(e)).
 
• **Freedom to practice any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade, or business** (Article 19(1)(g)).
 
 
 
• The freedoms granted under Article 19 are subject to certain "reasonable restrictions" imposed by the state, in the interest of **sovereignty, integrity, public order, decency, morality, or the security of the state**.
 
• These rights are fundamental in the sense that they are enforceable by the judiciary, and any law or order infringing upon them can be declared unconstitutional.
 
• The **Right to Freedom** is part of the **Fundamental Rights** enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, highlighting its critical role in ensuring individual liberty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32):**
 
 
• Article 32 allows citizens to move directly to the Supreme Court for the enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.
 
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to Article 32 as the "heart and soul" of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It provides remedies such as writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto) to enforce these rights.
 
 
 
• **Right to Education (Article 21A):**
 
 
• Inserted by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002**, this article provides the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.
 
• The **RTE Act, 2009** enforces this provision and ensures that every child has access to basic education.
 
 
 
• **Right to Information (RTI Act, 2005):**
 
 
• The RTI Act empowers citizens to request information from public authorities, promoting transparency and accountability in governance.
 
• It is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but is derived from the **Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression** (Article 19(1)(a)) and the Right to Life (Article 21).
 
 
 
• **Other Related Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• Part III of the Indian Constitution includes other critical rights like the **Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)** and the **Right Against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)**.
 
• These rights collectively aim to protect individual freedoms and promote social justice.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The freedoms under Article 19 are not absolute and can be restricted under specific conditions such as national security, public order, or morality.
 
• The judiciary plays a crucial role in interpreting and safeguarding these rights in case of disputes.
 
• Article 19 is applicable only to Indian citizens and not to foreigners.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following options does the Central Bank adopt in order to increase money supply?

options.text: It buys government securities in the open market
It increases the spending of the government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It buys government securities in the open market.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Central Bank, such as the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, uses the **Open Market Operations (OMO)** as a key monetary policy tool to regulate the money supply in the economy.
 
• When the Central Bank buys government securities in the open market, it injects liquidity into the banking system, thereby increasing the **money supply**. This is generally done to stimulate economic growth during periods of sluggish economic activity.
 
• Purchasing government securities results in more funds being available with commercial banks, which enhances their capacity to lend money to businesses and individuals, fostering investment and consumption.
 
• This action is part of an **expansionary monetary policy**, which aims to promote economic activity by encouraging borrowing and spending.
 
• Unlike other options mentioned in the question, this specific measure directly affects the money supply in the economy by increasing the availability of funds in the financial system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Open Market Operations (OMO):**
 
 
• OMO refers to the buying and selling of government securities in the open market by the Central Bank to control liquidity in the economy.
 
• When the Central Bank buys securities, it increases the money supply. Conversely, selling securities reduces the money supply, which is used to curb inflation.
 
• In India, the **RBI** conducts OMO under its monetary policy framework to achieve price stability and economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy Tools:**
 
 
• Aside from OMO, the Central Bank uses tools such as the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**, **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**, and **Repo Rate** to regulate the economy.
 
• For example, a reduction in the repo rate can encourage borrowing by reducing the cost of funds for banks.
 
 
 
• **Expansionary vs. Contractionary Policies:**
 
 
• An **expansionary monetary policy**, like buying government securities, aims to boost economic growth by increasing the money supply.
 
• A **contractionary monetary policy**, on the other hand, involves selling securities to reduce liquidity and control inflation.
 
 
 
• **Government Securities:**
 
 
• These are **debt instruments** issued by the government to finance its fiscal deficit and borrowing requirements.
 
• Examples of government securities in India include **Treasury Bills (T-bills)** and **Government Bonds**.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The Central Bank uses OMOs in coordination with other monetary tools to balance inflation and growth.
 
• For example, during the **COVID-19 pandemic**, the RBI purchased government securities to ensure adequate liquidity and support economic recovery.
 
 
</ul
